q:
בן 82, פנה לרופא המשפחה עקב אירועים חוזרים של התעלפות. ברקע - סובל מיתר ל"ד, השמנת יתר, סוכרת ודמנציה. תרופות קבועות:   
 RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)  
 LERCANIDIPINE (VASODIP)  
 MEMANTIN (MEMOX)  
 DONEPEZIL (MEMORIT)  
 ATORVASTATIN (LIPITOR  
 אקו לב שנעשה לפני חודשיים תקין. במסגרת בירור נעשה הולטר שהדגים קטעים מרובים של: איזו מהתרופות הבאות מסבירה את הממצא באק"ג?
o: RAMIPRIL (TRITACE)
LERCANIDIPINE ( VASODIP)
MEMANTIN ( MEMOX)
DONEPEZIL ( MEMORIT)
explanation:
A drug that slows sinus or atrioventricular conduction can cause a pause long enough to reduce cerebral perfusion and cause syncope. A normal echocardiogram does not exclude an intermittent electrical problem.

**Donepezil** increases vagal effects on the heart and best explains the pauses accompanying recurrent fainting.

**A. Ramipril.** This ACE inhibitor lowers blood pressure. Hypotension can cause lightheadedness but gives a different explanation from intermittent conduction pauses.
**B. Lercanidipine.** This dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker primarily dilates arteries. Marked nodal slowing is more characteristic of other calcium-channel blockers.
**C. Memantine.** This NMDA antagonist has a different mechanism and may be considered when bradycardia limits cholinesterase therapy.
**D. Donepezil.** Increasing acetylcholine can slow the sinus rate or cause heart block. Either can account for a symptomatic pause.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 911–913, 1143.

q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment has lost weight because of missed meals and low intake. Nutritional assessment finds that dietary restrictions are making intake difficult; he has no swallowing problem. Which plan is appropriate?
o: Increase dietary restrictions and concentrate food into one large meal
Reduce dietary restrictions and provide assistance with small meals
Increase dietary restrictions and reduce the number of daily meals
Reduce food variety and avoid snacks between regular meals
explanation:
Memory impairment can cause missed meals even when the patient can swallow safely. **Simplify unnecessary restrictions and arrange help with frequent small meals.**

**A. More restrictions and one large meal** — A single missed meal could remove most daily intake, and tighter rules make eating harder.
**B. Fewer restrictions and assisted small meals** — Cues and help address forgetfulness, while smaller, more frequent meals offer repeated chances to eat.
**C. More restrictions and fewer meals** — Both changes aggravate the barriers already identified.
**D. Narrow variety and avoid snacks** — Preferred foods and snacks can add energy when ordinary meals are inadequate.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 427, Table 30-11 and nonpharmacologic strategies.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: An 85-year-old man is being evaluated for delirium. A contributing medication has been identified and can be stopped after assessing its benefits and risks. What is consistent with the Hazzard management algorithm?
o: Continue the contributing drug and add a benzodiazepine for confusion
Discontinue the contributing drug as part of treating delirium causes
Increase the contributing drug to stabilize the patient's cognitive state
Delay changing the contributing drug until behavioral symptoms are treated
explanation:
A drug that impairs cognition is one treatable cause of delirium. Review its indication and withdrawal risk before choosing a change.
**Discontinue the contributing drug when it is safe to do so, and reassess symptoms and other contributors.**

**A. Continue the contributing drug and add a benzodiazepine for confusion.** Adding a benzodiazepine retains the trigger and may further impair attention.
**B. Discontinue the contributing drug as part of treating delirium causes.** Removal is appropriate here because the drug is dispensable after a benefits and risks assessment.
**C. Increase the contributing drug to stabilize the patient's cognitive state.** Increasing the exposure could intensify the adverse effect.
**D. Delay changing the contributing drug until behavioral symptoms are treated.** Cause-directed care should begin even while the team manages the patient's symptoms.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 885, 887, Figure 58-2

q: A transition to a different care setting is being planned for a person with dementia. Which feature should be preserved to reduce difficulty adapting to change?
o: Frequent changes in surroundings to encourage flexibility.
Frequent changes in caregivers to encourage flexibility.
Consistency in the care team and the environment.
Reduced contact with familiar caregivers and surroundings.
explanation:
People with dementia often have difficulty learning new routines and finding their way in unfamiliar surroundings. During a move, preserve familiar caregivers and environmental cues to help the person stay oriented and reduce distress.

**A. Change surroundings frequently.** Repeated room changes require the person to relearn where the bed or toilet is and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
**B. Rotate caregivers.** New staff may miss the person's usual way of communicating discomfort or a need for help.
**C. Keep caregivers and surroundings consistent.** Maintain contact with familiar staff or family and preserve recognizable objects and daily routines in the new setting.
**D. Reduce familiar contact.** Withdrawing trusted people removes reassurance just as the person is coping with a move.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 259.

q: An 89-year-old man with advanced Parkinson disease develops rigidity and fever after running out of carbidopa-levodopa and stopping it abruptly. Which medication change is the recognized trigger of a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome described by Hazzard?
o: Gradually adding an extra levodopa dose during the day
Moving a regular levodopa dose to a nearby time
Abruptly stopping the regular levodopa doses during the day
Dividing regular levodopa doses into smaller doses that day
explanation:
Someone with advanced Parkinson disease may depend on each levodopa dose to move. A sudden loss of dopaminergic treatment can cause a far more serious illness than the ordinary return of stiffness before a dose.

**Abruptly stopping regular levodopa can trigger a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.** Marked rigidity and fever after he ran out are the warning signs.

**A. Gradually add a dose.** This increases dopaminergic exposure and can cause peak-dose involuntary movements.
**B. Move a dose slightly.** A timing change may alter an off period. It does not reproduce sudden cessation of all treatment.
**C. Stop the regular doses abruptly.** The rapid fall in dopaminergic stimulation fits both the medication history and this severe presentation.
**D. Divide doses.** Smaller divided doses can smooth peaks when total exposure is maintained. The trigger here is withdrawal.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 946.
ref: Hazzard Ch 61 — PARKINSON DISEASE AND RELATED DISORDERS

q: An 81-year-old woman in assisted living is assessed because her care needs have increased. She has moderate Alzheimer disease, osteoporosis with a recent vertebral fracture, and urinary incontinence. Her caregiver reports new dependence in bathing and dressing, previously performed independently, and two falls this month. Her medicines are donepezil 10 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, and acetaminophen as needed. Which response to oxybutynin matches Beers 2023?
o: Continue oxybutynin because its adverse effects are confined to the urinary tract
Review oxybutynin for discontinuation because of adverse cognitive effects
Increase oxybutynin because stronger anticholinergic activity protects cognitive function
Switch bladder antimuscarinics because the cognitive warning does not extend across the class
explanation:
Oxybutynin treats bladder urgency by blocking muscarinic receptors. Cognitive adverse effects are particularly important in a patient with dementia and falls.

**Review stopping oxybutynin.** Its potential contribution to worsening function merits assessment alongside other causes.

**A. Continue because effects are confined to the bladder.** This drug also has central effects and can impair cognition.
**B. Review discontinuation.** Removing a strong anticholinergic can help assess how much the medication contributes to new functional problems.
**C. Increase for cognitive protection.** More muscarinic blockade can increase cognitive harm.
**D. Switch without cognitive review.** Other bladder antimuscarinics also warrant caution even though evidence of cognitive harm is strongest for oxybutynin.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, pp. 2066, 2074.

q: Duloxetine is being considered for a 76-year-old man with neuropathic pain and a calculated creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. Which approach follows the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Start the usual dose and monitor kidney function during treatment
Start a low dose and increase it gradually during treatment
Avoid duloxetine in the range of kidney function described
Give duloxetine intermittently while retaining the usual dose per administration
explanation:
Duloxetine is an SNRI used for neuropathic pain. **A creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min is below the 30 mL/min avoidance threshold.**

**A. Start the usual dose and monitor kidney function during treatment** Later laboratory surveillance cannot make an initial usual dose appropriate in this range.
**B. Start a low dose and increase it gradually during treatment** Slow titration helps tolerability in other settings. Here the recommendation is avoidance.
**C. Avoid duloxetine in the range of kidney function described** Choose an alternative that can be individualized for kidney function and fall risk.
**D. Give duloxetine intermittently while retaining the usual dose per administration** Intermittent use at the usual dose is not the recommended renal adjustment for duloxetine.

Reference · AGS Beers Criteria 2023, Table 6, p. 2073.

q: A 79-year-old woman with stress urinary incontinence begins conservative treatment with pelvic floor exercises but has difficulty understanding the technique. Which instruction matches Hazzard?
o: Practice repeated contractions of the pelvic floor muscles
Practice bearing down with the abdomen during each contraction
Perform a Valsalva maneuver to activate the pelvic muscles
Increase intra-abdominal pressure in place of contracting the muscles
explanation:
Pelvic-floor exercise strengthens the muscles that support urethral closure during exertion. **Teach repeated isolated squeezes with the abdomen relaxed.**

**A. Practice repeated contractions of the pelvic floor muscles** — Repeated contraction builds control. A clinician can check the squeeze during examination.
**B. Practice bearing down with the abdomen during each contraction** — Bearing down increases abdominal pressure and opposes the intended lift.
**C. Perform a Valsalva maneuver to activate the pelvic muscles** — A Valsalva maneuver increases bladder pressure and can provoke leakage.
**D. Increase intra-abdominal pressure in place of contracting the muscles** — Raising pressure without activating the pelvic floor challenges the outlet rather than strengthening it.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch. 47, pp. 709–710.

q: A 79-year-old woman with an osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture asks when vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty is considered in Hazzard. Which situation supports considering it?
o: Persistent severe pain attributed to the fracture despite conservative care
New severe fracture pain before a trial of conservative care
Persistent severe pain with a burst fracture and retropulsed bone
Persistent severe pain with an uncorrected coagulation disorder
explanation:
Vertebral augmentation uses cement to stabilize a fractured vertebral body. **Consider it when severe pain still localizes to the fracture despite a trial of conservative care.**

**A. Persistent severe fracture pain** Confirm that the fracture explains the pain, then discuss the uncertain magnitude of benefit and procedural risks.
**B. Severe pain at onset** Analgesia, activity modification and movement as tolerated are initial measures. Pain frequently improves as the fracture heals.
**C. Burst fracture with retropulsion** A displaced fragment can threaten the canal. This pattern requires assessment of stability and neural compression before considering intervention.
**D. Uncorrected coagulation disorder** A needle procedure involving the spine carries a bleeding risk. Address the coagulopathy before considering augmentation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Chapter 102, p. 1638 · CMS LCD L38201, vertebral augmentation, indications and limitations.

q: An older woman with unilateral renal artery stenosis and stable kidney function asks about a stent. Which statement agrees with the discussion of stable renal artery disease in Hazzard?
o: Revascularization is first-line treatment because trials show better outcomes than medical therapy.
Medical therapy is first-line treatment; CORAL found no benefit from revascularization.
Medical therapy is unsuitable because it does not improve blood pressure control.
Reduced filtration favors intervention because unilateral disease generally shows improved filtration.
explanation:
Stable atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis causes a visible narrowing, but opening the artery does not reliably improve patient outcomes. **Medical therapy is the initial approach** for stable unilateral disease.

**A. Revascularize first because outcomes improve** — Routine stenting did not improve the composite clinical outcome compared with medical management in CORAL.
**B. Begin with medical therapy** — Treat hypertension and associated vascular risks. In CORAL, adding revascularization offered no overall outcome advantage.
**C. Medical therapy cannot improve blood pressure** — Blood pressure control is a central aim of medical management and can often be achieved without a procedure.
**D. Reduced filtration usually improves after unilateral intervention** — When GFR is already moderately reduced in unilateral disease, intervention usually fails to restore it. Selected high-risk presentations require a separate assessment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1289, Renovascular Disease, Management.

q: An older man with postoperative delirium endangers himself and interrupts essential care despite nonpharmacologic measures. A short antipsychotic trial is being considered. What is its intended role in this setting?
o: Reduce mortality attributable to postoperative delirium
Control agitation that threatens safety and essential care
Shorten delirium duration by treating its underlying cause
Shorten the hospital stay by correcting the confusion
explanation:
For severe agitation, a short antipsychotic trial can be considered after supportive measures fail. Its purpose is immediate safety while separate treatment addresses the cause.
**Control behavior that threatens the patient or interrupts essential care.**

**A. Reduce mortality attributable to postoperative delirium.** Trials do not support prescribing an antipsychotic to reduce mortality from delirium.
**B. Control agitation that threatens safety and essential care.** Safe access to necessary treatment is the immediate behavioral goal.
**C. Shorten delirium duration by treating its underlying cause.** An antipsychotic does not reverse the precipitating illness or consistently shorten the syndrome.
**D. Shorten the hospital stay by correcting the confusion.** Length of stay is not a reliable pharmacologic treatment effect.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 888–889

q: An older woman with low-risk MDS is transfusion dependent. Cytogenetic testing shows an isolated deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5. Which treatment is the standard approach described for this subgroup?
o: Azacitidine to target the isolated 5q deletion
Lenalidomide to target the isolated 5q deletion
Stem-cell transplantation as routine treatment for the deletion
Transfusions in place of assessing deletion-directed treatment
explanation:
An isolated deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5 identifies an MDS subgroup with severe anemia and particular sensitivity to an immunomodulatory drug. **Use lenalidomide for transfusion-dependent lower-risk disease with isolated del(5q).**

**A. Azacitidine** — This hypomethylating agent has an important role in higher-risk MDS. It is not the deletion-directed choice here.
**B. Lenalidomide** — It can reduce transfusion needs and produce cytogenetic responses. Monitor counts for treatment-related myelosuppression.
**C. Routine transplantation** — Transplantation has substantial treatment-related risks and is reserved for selected candidates.
**D. Transfusions alone** — Transfusions relieve symptomatic anemia but leave a treatment-responsive clone unaddressed.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1485–1486, Table 95-4.
ref: Hazzard Ch 95 — HEMATOLOGIC MALIGNANCIES (LEUKEMIA/LYMPHOMA) AND PLASMA CELL DISORDERS
chapterTitle: HEMATOLOGIC MALIGNANCIES (LEUKEMIA/LYMPHOMA) AND PLASMA CELL DISORDERS

q: מטופל הגיע לאשפוז בעקבות אצירת שתן ובלבול לאחר שהתחיל לאחרונה תרופה נגד דיכאון. איזו תרופה סביר להניח שהתחיל לקבל?
o: CITALOPRAM (RECITAL)
ECITALOPRAM (CIPRALEX)
PAROXETIN (PAXXET)
LUSTRAL (SERTRALINE)
explanation:
Loss of attention and urinary retention after a new medication suggest antimuscarinic toxicity. Antidepressants in the same class differ in this respect.

**Paroxetine is the most likely of the four SSRIs to cause the combination.**

**A. Citalopram** QT prolongation and hyponatremia are more characteristic concerns than marked antimuscarinic toxicity.
**B. Escitalopram** Its anticholinergic activity is comparatively low.
**C. Paroxetine** Muscarinic blockade can impair bladder emptying and worsen confusion in a susceptible older patient.
**D. Sertraline** It can cause gastrointestinal symptoms or hyponatremia, but is less likely to explain urinary retention together with confusion.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 929–930, Table 60-9; AGS Beers Criteria 2023, Table 7
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: בת 72, אושפזה לצורך בירור בצקות ברגליים ועליה במשקל מזה מספר חודשים. במסגרת הבירור אובחנה שחמת ומיימת בכמות בינונית. מה הגישה המתאימה בנוגע ל- Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
o: אם אין רגישות בבדיקת בטן הסיכון ל- SBP נמוך מאד ויש צורך במעקב בלבד
אם אין חום ומדדי דלקת סיסטמי, מומלץ לטפל תסמינית במיימת ללא ניקור אבחנתי
לאחר ניקור להתחיל ROCEPHIN בשל טרנסלוקציה של חיידקים מהמעי לפריטונאום
לאחר ניקור להתחיל TAZOCIN בשל שיעור עמידויות גבוה של החיידקים
keySource: IMA 2026-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q137
chapterTitle: Harrison 22e ch. 355 – Cirrhosis and Its Complications
explanation:
Hospitalized patients with cirrhosis and new ascites need diagnostic paracentesis even without fever or tenderness. **Send cell count with differential and culture. An ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/µL supports SBP and warrants prompt empiric treatment without awaiting culture**, unless another intra-abdominal cause explains the inflammation.

**A. Nontender abdomen means observe.** SBP can be clinically subtle, so a nontender examination is not enough to avoid sampling.
**B. No fever means treat only ascites.** Afebrile patients can still have infected ascites. Cell count and culture guide management.
**C. Ceftriaxone after the tap.** A third-generation cephalosporin is appropriate for suspected or confirmed community-acquired SBP. Treat promptly when clinical suspicion is strong, especially in an unstable patient. New ascites alone does not require antibiotics after every tap.
**D. Routine piperacillin–tazobactam.** Broader coverage depends on healthcare exposure, local resistance and severity.

Reference · Harrison 22e, pp. 329, 2715–2716. AASLD guidance on ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, 2021.

Key note: The official key credits ceftriaxone after paracentesis. Harrison calls for diagnostic sampling of new ascites and treats SBP with a third-generation cephalosporin. The stem supplies neither an ascitic neutrophil count nor another finding that establishes suspected SBP. Chapter 53 defines SBP at ≥250 neutrophils/µL (p. 329). Chapter 355 prints >250/µL (pp. 2715–2716).

q:
בת 82, מתגוררת בביתה. ברקע: מחלת לב איסכמית, יתר לחץ דם, תת פעילות של בלוטת התריס, אוסטיאופורוזיס ומצב לאחר שחזור וקיבוע מפרק הירך מימין לפני כשנתיים על רקע שבר אינטרטרוכנטרי.
אושפזה עקב כאב ואודם מקומי באזור הניתוח. בבדיקה נצפה סינוס מפריש מעל הצלקת הניתוחית. לאחר השלמת בירור מעבדתי ודימות CT עולה חשד לזיהום המשתל (Periprosthetic Joint Infection). בתרבית מההפרשה נמצא Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA). לאורך אשפוזה עד כה המטופלת יציבה המודינמית ונשימתית, ללא חום וללא סימני ספסיס.
מה מהבאים נכון בהתייחס לאבחנה במקרה זה?
o: שקיעת הדם המוחשת שנמדדה במהלך אשפוזה הינה ספציפית אך לא רגישה
בדיקת מיפוי עצם (Bone scan) הינה בדיקה רגישה יותר מבדיקת ה- CT לאבחנת הזיהום במשתל במטופלת זו
סף האבחנה (Threshold values) של זיהום משתל מפרקי בכל המפרקים הוא מעל 1700 תאים/ מ"ל
Staphylococcus Aureus הוא המזהם השכיח בזיהומי משתלים מאוחרים
keySource: IMA 2022-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q106
explanation:
A draining sinus communicating with hardware or bone strongly supports implant-related infection. **Bone scintigraphy can be sensitive to abnormal turnover, but it is nonspecific.** Intertrochanteric fracture fixation can leave screws or a nail rather than a prosthetic joint. Establish which operation she had and obtain reliable deep specimens.

**A. ESR specific but insensitive.** ESR and CRP are nonspecific inflammatory markers. Neither confirms nor excludes deep infection by itself.
**B. Bone scan more sensitive than CT.** CT may be limited by metal artifact and can show collections or anatomy. A positive bone scan can reflect remodeling as well as infection. Neither determines the organism.
**C. One synovial threshold in every joint.** Cutoffs depend on joint, timing and context, and are usually expressed as cells per µL, not per mL. They may not apply to fracture-fixation hardware.
**D. S. aureus is most common in late infections.** It is prominent in acute hematogenous infections. Indolent implant infections often involve coagulase-negative staphylococci. MRSA on a drainage swab does not prove the deep pathogen.

Reference · Harrison 22e, pp. 1060, 1066. Fracture-Related Infection Consensus Group, Diagnosing Fracture-Related Infection: Current Concepts and Recommendations, 2020.
